text:
Maya: Quick follow-up from the CP separation RFC — curious if folks are ok with moving to a stitchless credential-swap for private endpoints. The idea: no persistent peering for controlplane, we use a short-lived per-tenant credential exchange + local agent keepalive to avoid long-lived network peering. Advantages: simpler network rules, fewer VPCs to manage, cheaper for low-traffic tenants. Downsides: more auth traffic and slightly more controlplane hops when agents reconnect. Thoughts?

Simon: I'm +1 on avoiding long-lived peering where we can. Two questions: 1) how are we doing auth rotation? 2) what's expected reconnection latency impact for small bursts?

Maya: rotation: short-lived signed tokens minted by CP with audience=tenant-agent, TTL ~5m. Agents refresh via an authenticated endpoints over privatelink (or mgmt relay). Reconnect: we expect an extra 1-2 RTTs for the credential exchange, so ~100-200ms median for reconnect, but steady-state requests are unchanged because KV cache stays local.

Alex: Quick perf note — if we rely on token minting for every reconnect, we need a light path that doesn't hit heavy DB queries. Suggest a token cache in the CP front tier (L1) and a rate limit bucket per-tenant. Also need to ensure KMS calls for signing are batched or proxied.

Patrick: Operational concerns: rollback surface if token-service has a bug. We should support a short canary rollout (1% tenants) + fallback to peering for tenants that opt-in. Also need observability: token mint latency, token fail rate, agent reconnect histogram. Without that we'll be blind.

Maya: Agree. Plan sketch: A) token microservice (stateless, caches tenant meta), B) CP front-tier L1 caches tokens and does signing using a signer-proxy that uses HSM/KMS (no per-request remote KMS), C) agents support fallback to peering if token exchange fails twice in a row.

Simon: How do we map tenant identity into the token? Right now peering uses VPC-level isolation. With stitchless we need to ensure network+identity both considered. Suggest token payload include tenant_id + allowed-controlplane-scopes + allowed-egress-prefixes. Then CP enforces scope on subsequent requests.

Maya: Yep, that's the thought. Token example: ```{
  "sub": "tenant:acme-corp",
  "exp": 1710000000,
  "scopes": ["control.read","control.exec"],
  "egress": ["10.2.0.0/16"]
}``` Signed with KMS key. Agent uses it to open mTLS with CP front-tier and CP validates.

Alex: One more: backup path for high-throughput tenants. If a tenant has >X sustained qps, we can auto-provision a peering or dedicated connector and surface that in billing. That avoids auth churn.

Patrick: Rollout checklist suggestion: 1) unit tests + integration harness for token-service, 2) synthetic reconnect load test, 3) 1% canary on staging tenants, 4) expand to 10% with telemetry gates, 5) manual opt-in for dedicated peering.

Maya: Sounds good. I'll draft a short RFC addendum with the token format, signer-proxy design, and the rollout checklist. @Simon @Alex @Patrick if you can add any missed failure modes (esp. PKI/KMS edge cases) that'd be great.

deploy-bot: deploy queued: token-service:v2 -> canary (1%) :hourglass_flowing_sand:

Simon: :thumbsup: thanks, this approach feels like a nice middle ground between full peering and pure public CP.

Alex: Adding a note — we should audit egress CID matching logic; mistakes there are high blast. I'll open a quick PR after the addendum.

Patrick: I'll add the observability dashboards to the rollout ticket.

Maya: Thanks all — will share the addendum in #architecture when ready.
